transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Yeah, um… I guess what finally pushed me to come in is I can’t keep my focus the way I need to. I’m an electrician, so a lot of what I do is estimates, code forms, planning out jobs, making sure the right materials are going to the right site — stuff where you really can’t be bouncing all over the place.

Lately I’ll sit down to finish one estimate, and then some tool noise in the shop, or my phone buzzing with a text, or even just some new idea about reorganizing the workshop or changing how I’m doing a job will pull me completely off track. And then I’m halfway into something else before I even realize I never finished the first thing.

It’s gotten to where jobs start getting mixed up — like paperwork, materials, details — and that’s not like me, or at least it can’t keep happening. I kept telling myself I just needed to buckle down, but it’s like my attention gets yanked away constantly, and I’m having a hard time getting it back.
Before age 12, were you already having trouble paying attention or staying organized?

Honestly, I don’t really know. I mean, I was a kid, so it’s hard for me to separate what was normal kid stuff from an actual problem. I don’t remember it being some big thing where teachers were constantly saying I couldn’t pay attention or anything like that, at least not that sticks out.

I can remember being messy sometimes, losing track of homework here and there, but I don’t know if that was more than anybody else. My parents might remember better than I do. For me, this feels more like something I’m noticing as a real problem now because my work depends on staying organized and following through.
Have you had a period where you felt unusually energized or wired compared with your normal self?

Yeah… yeah, I have. That’s actually part of what’s been weird, because it’s not just “I had coffee and I’m busy.” It’s like I get this engine running in me and I’m just going nonstop.

Like I’ll finish at a job site, and instead of calling it for the day I’ll go straight into looking at bids, then I’ll end up in the workshop rewiring some test panel or messing with a setup because I suddenly think of a better way to do it. And then I’ll start some whole home-automation idea — like sensors, lighting controls, whatever — before I’ve even finished the last thing I started.

It feels productive in the moment, like sitting still is almost… I don’t know, like I’m wasting time or falling behind. So I keep moving from one thing to the next, and at first it feels kind of great because I’m getting stuff done, or at least starting a lot of stuff. But it’s definitely more wired than my normal self.
When you get into those unusually energized or wired periods, do you need less sleep than usual?

Yeah. Definitely. That’s been one of the stranger parts, honestly, because I’ve always needed a normal night of sleep to function, you know? But for months now, when I get into that mode, I’ll sleep maybe three or four hours and then I’m just… up. Like before dawn, wide awake, and not in that groggy, miserable way where you’re dragging yourself out of bed.

I’ll wake up and my brain is already going — like, “Okay, I should price those materials,” or “I can answer those emails now before everyone else is up,” or I’ll start sketching out some new system layout, like lighting controls or whatever idea I had the night before. And it feels like I slept a full night, even though I can look at the clock and know I absolutely didn’t.

It’s not like I’m lying there wishing I could sleep more, at least not at first. I just pop up and feel ready to go, which sounds useful, but it’s also kind of unnerving when I step back and realize I’m running on three or four hours like it’s nothing.
During those wired periods, do you feel more confident or capable than usual?

Yeah… I do. And it’s not just regular confidence, like “I’m good at my job.” I mean, I do think I’m good at electrical work, but during those periods it gets bigger than that.

I’ll start thinking I can take on commercial jobs, like bigger projects than I would normally even seriously bid on. I’ll be looking at something and thinking, “I could handle that. I could run that. I could get a crew together and train them up and we’d knock it out.” And in the moment it feels completely obvious, like I’m seeing this path that other people aren’t seeing.

But then there’s this other part of me — not always loud enough, but it’s there — that knows my licensing and experience aren’t exactly where they need to be for some of that. Like, I’ve got skills, I’m not saying I don’t, but there’s a difference between being capable on the tools and being ready to run a whole commercial operation with a crew under me. When I’m in that wired mode, though, that difference doesn’t feel as important. It feels like I can just figure it out as I go, and that confidence gets pretty intense.
During those wired periods, do you find yourself talking more than usual?

I’m not totally sure on that one. I mean… I probably talk more when I’m in that state just because I’m doing more and I’ve got more ideas bouncing around, but I haven’t really tracked it the way I’ve noticed the sleep or the whole taking-on-too-much thing.

Like, if I’m explaining a job or talking through an idea, I can definitely go on for a while — but I also kind of do that normally if it’s something I’m interested in. So it’s hard for me to say, “Yes, that’s a clear thing that changes.” Nobody’s really sat me down and said, “You’re talking nonstop,” or anything like that.

I guess what I notice more is that my thoughts feel faster, and if someone asks me about something I’m working on, I might dump the whole plan on them. But whether I’m actually talking way more than usual… I don’t know. Maybe a little, but I’m not confident saying it’s a big symptom for me.
During those wired periods, do you do things that are unusually risky or impulsive for you?

I’m not sure, honestly. I mean, I don’t think of myself as a reckless person, so when you say “risky,” my first reaction is kind of, “No, not really,” but then I’m also wondering what counts.

Like, I don’t have some clear story where I’m suddenly doing something totally out of character and everyone around me is like, “What are you doing?” At least not that I can point to easily. During those wired times I might make faster decisions, or feel more ready to jump into something, but I’m not sure if I’d call it risky exactly, or just… me being more keyed up and confident.

Impulsive, maybe in small ways? Like I might not sit with a decision as long as I normally would. But I don’t know that I’ve noticed a big pattern of dangerous stuff or anything like that. It’s harder for me to answer than the sleep thing, because with sleep I can look at the clock. With this, it’s more like… I’d probably need someone else to tell me if I’m crossing a line.
After those wired periods, do you then go through a time when your mood drops and you feel depressed?

I’m not really sure how to answer that cleanly. I mean, I definitely have times after where I feel worn out or kind of embarrassed looking back at how intense I was, like, “Why was I so sure about all that?” But I don’t know if I’d call it a real depression or a mood drop in the way you mean.

Sometimes it’s more like I come back down to normal and then I’m dealing with whatever I said yes to, or whatever I got myself excited about, and that can feel heavy. But I haven’t really tracked it as a clear pattern, like wired period and then definitely depressed after. It’s not as obvious to me as the wired part itself.

So… maybe there’s a crash sometimes, but I can’t honestly say, “Yes, every time after that I get depressed.” I’d have to think about it more, or maybe ask someone close to me if they’ve noticed that pattern.
During those wired periods, has it ever gotten bad enough that it caused serious problems at work or home, or that someone thought you needed emergency help?

Yeah… I mean, I wouldn’t say it’s gotten to the point where someone dragged me to the ER or anything like that. Nobody’s called an ambulance or said I needed emergency help, at least not in that dramatic kind of way.

But serious problems? Yeah, I think I have to admit that. It’s been affecting work more than I want to say out loud. I’m an electrician, so details matter — schedules, parts, who’s going where, what got finished, what still needs checking — and during those wired stretches I’ll be moving fast and taking on a lot, but then details get missed or mixed up. I’ve had clients complain because something wasn’t lined up right, or I told them one timing and then it turned out I’d scheduled something else on top of it. And that’s embarrassing, because I’ve built a lot of my reputation on being reliable.

And my apprentices… that’s been hard too. They don’t seem to trust my direction the way they used to. Like, I can tell they’re second-guessing whether I actually have the plan straight, or whether I’m changing things on them too fast. I don’t like admitting that, because I’m supposed to be the one they can count on.

At home it’s probably been worse in a different way. My wife and I argue about the mortgage and the business a lot now. She feels like I’m putting everything we built at risk, and I get defensive because in the moment I feel like I’m trying to grow things or fix things or make something happen. But I can see why it scares her. So… yeah, not emergency-help bad, but it’s definitely caused real problems at work and at home.
When one of these unusually wired periods happens, does it usually last at least four days in a row?

Yeah… I think so. I mean, I haven’t been marking it on a calendar, which I probably should have been, but it’s not like it’s just one afternoon where I’m wound up and then I sleep it off. It feels like these stretches have been going on for days at a time.

And honestly, the bigger thing is that this whole pattern has been building for about seven months now, since we took on the mortgage for the workshop and the equipment. That’s kind of the point where everything started feeling more pressured, and these wired spells started being more noticeable. So when you ask “four days in a row,” I’d say yes, usually it’s at least that long — or at least it feels that way from inside it. It’s not quick. It lingers.
During those wired periods, do other people clearly notice that you’re not acting like your usual self?

Yeah, they do. I mean, I don’t always see it while I’m in it, because at the time it feels like I’m just motivated or finally seeing the big picture, you know? But other people definitely react like I’m not quite myself.

I’ll get into this really pumped-up mode where I’m talking like our little shop is right on the edge of becoming the main solar outfit in town, like we’re about to take over that whole side of the market if everybody would just get on board and move fast enough. And I’ll be saying it with total confidence, like it’s obvious and everyone else is just not seeing it yet.

But then if my wife questions the numbers, or one of the apprentices asks whether the plan actually makes sense, I can turn sharp really quickly. Like, way sharper than the situation calls for. I’ll snap at them or talk over them, and afterward I can see why they looked at me like, “What is going on with you?” At the time I feel like they’re slowing me down or doubting me, but yeah… they notice. My wife definitely notices, and the guys at work notice too.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated/wired periods cause marked functional impairment or require hospitalization, which helps distinguish bipolar spectrum illness from ADHD/anxiety or less severe mood symptoms.
doctor.question: During those wired periods, has it ever gotten bad enough that it caused serious problems at work or home, or that someone thought you needed emergency help?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: Clients have started complaining about missed details and mixed-up scheduling, and my apprentices don’t trust my direction the way they used to. At home, the mortgage and the business are turning into constant arguments because my wife feels like I’m putting everything we built at risk.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the wired periods have caused serious problems at work or home or required emergency help, which is most directly about functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I mean, I wouldn’t say it’s gotten to the point where someone dragged me to the ER or anything like that. Nobody’s called an ambulance or said I needed emergency help, at least not in that dramatic kind of way.

But serious problems? Yeah, I think I have to admit that. It’s been affecting work more than I want to say out loud. I’m an electrician, so details matter — schedules, parts, who’s going where, what got finished, what still needs checking — and during those wired stretches I’ll be moving fast and taking on a lot, but then details get missed or mixed up. I’ve had clients complain because something wasn’t lined up right, or I told them one timing and then it turned out I’d scheduled something else on top of it. And that’s embarrassing, because I’ve built a lot of my reputation on being reliable.

And my apprentices… that’s been hard too. They don’t seem to trust my direction the way they used to. Like, I can tell they’re second-guessing whether I actually have the plan straight, or whether I’m changing things on them too fast. I don’t like admitting that, because I’m supposed to be the one they can count on.

At home it’s probably been worse in a different way. My wife and I argue about the mortgage and the business a lot now. She feels like I’m putting everything we built at risk, and I get defensive because in the moment I feel like I’m trying to grow things or fix things or make something happen. But I can see why it scares her. So… yeah, not emergency-help bad, but it’s definitely caused real problems at work and at home.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the unusually energized periods last at least 4 days, which is key to distinguishing a bipolar spectrum episode from ADHD, anxiety, adjustment disorder, or unipolar depression.
doctor.question: When one of these unusually wired periods happens, does it usually last at least four days in a row?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been building for about seven months, since we took on the mortgage for the workshop and equipment.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking how long the unusually wired periods last, which is directly about duration.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I think so. I mean, I haven’t been marking it on a calendar, which I probably should have been, but it’s not like it’s just one afternoon where I’m wound up and then I sleep it off. It feels like these stretches have been going on for days at a time.

And honestly, the bigger thing is that this whole pattern has been building for about seven months now, since we took on the mortgage for the workshop and the equipment. That’s kind of the point where everything started feeling more pressured, and these wired spells started being more noticeable. So when you ask “four days in a row,” I’d say yes, usually it’s at least that long — or at least it feels that way from inside it. It’s not quick. It lingers.

target_item.name: Elevated_Irritable_Mood
target_item.manifestation: I’ll be in this big, pumped-up mood talking like our little shop is about to become the main solar outfit in town, but if my wife or one of the apprentices questions the plan I can flip and get sharp with them over nothing.
target_item.reason: The question is asking whether the wired mood/behavior is clearly observable to others as a change from usual self, which most directly relates to the distinct elevated or irritable mood during these periods.

patient.answer:
Yeah, they do. I mean, I don’t always see it while I’m in it, because at the time it feels like I’m just motivated or finally seeing the big picture, you know? But other people definitely react like I’m not quite myself.

I’ll get into this really pumped-up mode where I’m talking like our little shop is right on the edge of becoming the main solar outfit in town, like we’re about to take over that whole side of the market if everybody would just get on board and move fast enough. And I’ll be saying it with total confidence, like it’s obvious and everyone else is just not seeing it yet.

But then if my wife questions the numbers, or one of the apprentices asks whether the plan actually makes sense, I can turn sharp really quickly. Like, way sharper than the situation calls for. I’ll snap at them or talk over them, and afterward I can see why they looked at me like, “What is going on with you?” At the time I feel like they’re slowing me down or doubting me, but yeah… they notice. My wife definitely notices, and the guys at work notice too.

inference.note: Sustained periods of elevated/irritable mood with decreased need for sleep, increased goal-directed activity, grandiosity, duration >=4 days, clear change noticed by others, and work/home impairment strongly support bipolar spectrum with hypomanic/manic symptoms. This makes ADHD/anxiety/adjustment/depressive disorder less likely as primary explanations based on current history.

opening_question.intent: Learn the patient's main reason for seeking care today
opening_question.question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes distinct periods of abnormally increased energy/wired mood lasting at least 4 days, with decreased need for sleep, inflated confidence/grandiosity, increased goal-directed activity, distractibility, faster thoughts, and observable change from baseline causing clear work and home impairment. This supports a bipolar spectrum disorder with hypomanic episodes. Full manic syndrome requiring emergency care or psychotic features was not established, and major depressive episodes were not clearly confirmed, making other bipolar disorder (F31.8) the best fit among the available options rather than unspecified bipolar disorder.
